lesson.title: Single-Blind: One Side Kept in the Dark
lesson.summary: In a single-blind experiment, the subjects do not know which treatment they are receiving, but the researchers who administer treatments or evaluate outcomes do know.
lesson.body:
A single-blind experiment applies blinding to exactly one of the two groups of people who could distort results: the subjects. In this design, the people receiving treatment have no way of knowing whether they are in the treatment group or the control group, but the researchers running the study, administering the pills, recording the doses, and often scoring the outcomes, know exactly who is who. The word single refers to counting the blinded parties, not to counting treatments; a single-blind study can compare any number of treatment groups, as long as only the subjects are kept uninformed.

This design directly attacks the placebo effect and other forms of subject-driven response bias. If a subject does not know she received the real drug rather than a placebo, her reported pain level, mood, or side effects cannot be shaped by the belief that she is being treated. Because subjects remain unaware, single-blinding neutralizes exactly the psychological mechanism described in the discussion of blinding: expectation quietly becoming data. It is a meaningful step up from an unblinded study, where subjects who know they are getting the real treatment may over-report improvement out of hope or a desire to please the researcher.

Single-blinding, however, leaves an opening that double-blinding closes: the researcher's own expectations remain unmanaged. A nurse who knows a participant is in the real-drug group might, without any intent to cheat, spend more time reassuring that participant, ask about symptoms in a more leading way, or interpret an ambiguous test result slightly more favorably. This is not fraud, it is ordinary human bias operating on people who sincerely want their hypothesis to be supported. Single-blind designs are common in situations where blinding the researcher is impractical, for instance when a therapist delivering counseling obviously knows which technique they are using, even if the client does not know which technique is considered the experimental one.

Consider a hypothetical study on whether a new labeling scheme reduces snack calorie consumption. Researchers give 60 participants identical bags of chips, but half the bags carry a red high calorie warning sticker while the other half carry no sticker; participants do not know the study is measuring stickers versus consumption, so their eating behavior is not shaped by trying to guess the hypothesis. The researcher recording how much each participant eats, however, knows exactly which bag each person received. If that researcher rounds calorie estimates differently depending on which group a participant is in, evaluator bias creeps back into the results even though the subjects themselves were fully blinded.

Single-blind experiments are a genuine improvement over no blinding at all, and they are sometimes the most rigorous design that is ethically or logistically possible. But when a study's outcome depends on subjective measurement, a symptom rating, a behavioral score, a diagnostic read, researchers generally want to close the remaining gap by blinding themselves as well, which is exactly the idea behind a double-blind experiment.
